utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Robinson. You have something to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you very much, Mr. President, and good morning. Mr. Tieger and I have been discussing this morning the issue of Rule 70 and its application to the testimony of General Smith as it relates to the events on the 27th of May, and we think that we should probably go into private session for this part of the discussion, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to note that we are sitting without Judge Lattanzi, who is not with us, due to urgent matters, for the rest of the week. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: You recall that yesterday an issue came up concerning -- whether testimony about the incident at the Vrbanja Bridge on the 27th of May, 1995, had to be heard in private session. And this morning, Mr. Tieger has given me a copy of a letter that was sent to us on the 5th of February, 2010, and it may be that the Chamber would also benefit from seeing this letter if, during the course of my remarks, you think it's a good idea, I can hand up my copy. But in the letter, it says that the witness statement of Rupert Smith, dated the 22nd of October, 2009, is being disclosed to us, and there is one condition, and that is that under paragraph 134 of the statement, we're not to disclose that to any other third parties. And I haven't seen that statement yet, but I assume that paragraph 134 relates to the events of the Vrbanja Bridge. But we don't believe that, first of all, this means that any testimony by General Smith about this topic is covered by this Rule 70 agreement. We note that we subsequently received an amalgamated statement earlier this year, and it contains several paragraphs relating to the result of the Vrbanja Bridge, and no condition was placed on our disclosure or dissemination of the information concerning that. In addition, the incidents at the Vrbanja Bridge are covered by numerous documents that we intend to use during our cross-examination that have been disclosed to us by the United Nations with no Rule 70 conditions, and so we don't -- while this witness statement that was covered by Rule 70, we don't intend to use that, and maybe that -- any questions about that witness statement should be in private session. We don't think that the Rule 70 provider is entitled to or has, even, insisted that all discussion of this Vrbanja Bridge incident be held in private session. And if they did, then we believe that that would be a condition that would infringe upon the right of the accused, and we would ask for an exclusion of General Smith's testimony as a result of that, because essentially you're allowing the evidence that the Bosnian Serbs took hostages and keeping from the public evidence that the UN also took four Serbs as prisoners and negotiated their exchange. So we don't think that that would be fair, to have that kind of slanted presentation for the public about the events that are the subject of Count 11. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we have a copy of that letter, in the meantime. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is relatively straightforward and, I believe, is being unduly complicated by the Defence at this point. A couple of points of clarification. First of all, it's not a Rule 70 agreement. Information was provided on that basis, and the Rule 70 provider, as the Court is well aware, frequently places restrictions on the information that it releases. Secondly, this is a trial, not a public relations effort, and the reality is the Court will be fully informed about the events, to the extent that it's possible through witnesses, by virtue of the fact that this information has been released so that it can be discussed with the Court, albeit in private session. The distinction that Mr. Robinson attempts to draw between the nature of the release with respect to the witness statement, at a time when it was anticipated that the witness's testimony would be given in this fashion is a specious one. It's quite clear that we believe, from reading this, that the restriction is as stated on the information related to that narrow topic, and we're simply attempting to abide by the provider's restrictions. In any event, the impact on the fairness of this trial is not only negligible, it's non-existent, and this is, I think, a highly unrealistic attempt to inflate this issue into something it's not. As Mr. Robinson noted, this matter will be -- to the extent it's important, it's going to be raised by the Defence. They'll be talking about it. There's no restriction on what they can talk about. They will have the benefit, in fact, of whatever information this witness may have to provide the Court, and can rely on that to whatever extent they think is useful, and can refer to it in an appropriate fashion, since it would have been elicited in private session. But to the extent it's significant that the -- to the Defence that they alert the public to this issue, they're going to do so. There's no restriction on discussing the incident to the extent they're aware of it. The only restriction here is on citation to this witness's evidence and identification of or release of that information in public. As the Court is well aware, the Tribunal deals with this issue constantly, and references are made in final arguments and in closing briefs to propositions that are supported by information elicited in private session, but the subject-matter of which is openly discussed generally, and the citations are appropriately safeguarded. This is not a problem and shouldn't be inflated into one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following this in its entirety. What information is it that was provided pursuant to Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, this witness is a Rule 70 witness, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow that this witness is a Rule 70 witness. Is this witness provided by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we had to -- we have to seek clearance for such witnesses from the UN, and we do so. And the only restriction on this witness's information and testimony is the one indicated. Other restrictions by the provider could have been imposed, or presumably, you know, much more significant than the narrow one we're considering at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in order to hear the evidence of this witness, you had to get the clearance of the United Nations, and the United Nations put that condition?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that condition being -- could you repeat what the condition was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It relates to information -- information regarding the detention of four individuals by UNPROFOR, which in this case refers to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because we don't have that paragraph, we don't have the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that information regarding the -- regarding the detention of the four individuals is contained in the paragraph, but the paragraph is broader than that, so it's sort of a reference point for that. And the statement says: "We held --" In the middle of the paragraph, it states: "We held four Bosnian Serb prisoners, and they held hundreds of ours. They had surrounded who were people besieged ...," et cetera, as he goes on to other parts of the information in the paragraph which are not the subject of this restriction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify what you meant when you said there's no restriction on discussing the incident to the extent they are aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Defence can ask other witnesses for whom there are no restrictions about it. They can call witnesses about this incident. They can argue the incident. I mean, this restriction wouldn't impose any barriers on that. This is a restriction related to the information provided by this witness only. And before I -- I would also note that with respect to the document that gave rise to this discussion, that was also provided on condition it be used in private session. But with respect to other witnesses, and for whom there are no related similar restrictions, of course, the issue can be probed to the extent the Defence considers appropriate. And Mr. Robinson has also -- has already alluded to the fact that he's aware of documents that don't have such restrictions and will come in publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have that witness statement dated 22nd of October in e-court? Can we up-load it so that we can -- or could you hand over the copy so that we can take a look, if it is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think it's in e-court, Your Honour. For the Registrar's benefit, it would be 22686.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This one is dated as 25th-26th June and September 21st. It has no comment about Vrbanja Bridge incident at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I wanted to clarify that, Your Honour, in a sense. So there's no -- there's no restriction on discussion of the Vrbanja Bridge incident. That's quite correct. However, in this -- the restriction is with regard to four persons detained. But parsing that out is rather difficult. So certainly someone alerted to those restricted guided by questions which took account of that distinction could ask questions publicly about the Vrbanja Bridge incident. But since that would -- that might well quickly lead into the eliciting of information that four persons were detained as a result of and the aftermath of that incident, it's quite difficult to imagine precisely how -- or in what context that would be discussed without intruding upon the issue of the four detained persons. But clearly, theoretically and in the abstract, there's no restriction on discussing the incident at the Vrbanja Bridge. The concern would be the extent to which you could do that without then entering into a discussion of or eliciting information about the four detained persons. So I think the Court's quite right, there is a distinction. But in a practical sense, it might be a hard one to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's difficult, what the condition was, actually. Having read this paragraph -- before that, why was it that the Court was not notified of such condition before we started hearing evidence of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, both parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the one option was not to hear this witness's evidence at all, if the Court was to find that that condition is not fair and in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you've heard our position on its fairness. We would have expected to be alerted to any view to the contrary by the Defence, having had possession of this information for approximately one year, so this was not and could not have been anticipated as any kind of problem, nor should it be a problem. I agree, it's a matter that the Court, under other circumstances, might need to resolve, but there was no indication here that there was such a problem that needed to be brought to the Court's attention. And I still consider that it is not a problem of any -- of such magnitude that it should be taking as much time as it is. In other words, it was only belatedly brought to our attention that the Defence had any concerns about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: According to this correspondence from the Prosecution to the Defence, it says like this: "Please be advised that the statement of this witness is provided under the following conditions which relates to information regarding the detention of four individuals by UNPROFOR contained in para 134 of said statement." So as far as these four individuals are concerned, that should be discussed under Rule 70 conditions. That's all what you were told by the United Nations; nothing else about -- which is contained in 134; for example, the first sentence -- or second sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is very imprecise, and I think we would all be aided by seeing the written correspondence between the United Nations and the Prosecution in which they placed the condition on -- the first question I think that I asked Dr. Karadzic to ask about this topic was did they have the consent of the Bosnian Serbs, and this is also covered by this paragraph. So this is very vague as to what exactly the Rule 70 provider has requested as a condition. I think you ought to see some documentation on that so we know exactly, first of all, what is the scope of the requested condition so you can enforce that, and then you can, secondly, decide whether enforcing that would make the trial unfair and deprive Dr. Karadzic of his right to a public trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In this regard, I usually take the words of the Prosecution. But as indicated by Mr. Robinson, it was the condition which was put in relation to this witness doesn't seem to be clear to the Court. So could you reiterate what the condition was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's regarding the information regarding the detention of four individuals by UNPROFOR in that paragraph. As you see in the paragraph, Your Honour, the disclosure of that information is strictly limited to the accused, his counsel and expert advisors, and the Tribunal, and the accused's counsel and expert advisors are prohibited from divulging that information to the media or any third party. And in the event that the witness statement comes into evidence, the reference in that paragraph should not form part of the public trial record. We're now in trial, eliciting information for the record, and that's why we sought to move into private session, in accordance with that condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not clear - Mr. Tieger and Mr. Robinson could help us - how the Vrbanja Bridge incident and the detention of four individuals are related.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think you'll see the backdrop in -- well, the backdrop is contained, in fact, in this witness's amalgamated statement, as well as others. But there was an incident during which Bosnian Serb soldiers attacked a French contingent on the Vrbanja Bridge, during which some French soldiers were wounded and killed. Then there was a re-taking of the bridge, during which the Bosnian Serb -- some Bosnian Serb soldiers who had taken that position were then detained. And as Mr. Robinson previously indicated, that occurred on the 27th of May. And during the telephone call between the witness and General Mladic on the 28th of May, which we began to look at yesterday - that was 65 ter, I think, 0315 or something - there is reference to both the incident and to the detained Serb -- Bosnian Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, can we discuss paragraph 128 in public session? Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand what the Court is pointing to. I think it would be unfair to the -- and I looked at that and considered all those possibilities, but I think it would be unfair to the provider to suggest that the reference to paragraph 134, by way of identifying the issue, was -- did not encompass any other references to the same information. I appreciate there may be -- there may seem to be an inconsistency there, but I don't think we would -- we could consider it a fair interpretation of the condition to suggest that the manner in which they identified the information which needed to be restricted, and which I think they identified it clearly, is trumped by another reference to the same information that they didn't happen to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your suggestion is to hear this evidence in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's in keeping with the provider's restriction. And we, of course, try to abide by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are sort of disappointed to be informed of such condition that existed, depriving -- being deprived of any opportunity to clarify or rectify to a certain extent, but for a practical solution the Chamber finds it best to proceed under that condition; i.e., we hear any questions and answers about the Vrbanja Bridge in private session. And then we'll see whether we can make some parts of those portions public; for example, the transcript that does not mention any of the four Serbs being detained by the UNPROFOR. And then we'll see whether we can do anything about this later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, was there simply the fact that four soldiers were detained not already in the public domain as a result of being reported at or about the time that it happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So that the mere fact that four people were detained, and the time which they were detained, is already, as it were, in the public domain?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And if I'm not mistaken, it may already be part of the public record in this case, at least to some extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's what I'm thinking. Without having the opportunity to check it, I wanted to see if it accorded with your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it the parties understood the Court's intention. We'll hear --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just say, for the record, one thing? It seems to me "quod licet iovi, non licet bovi" and I do not feel equal at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're not prohibited from asking any question. That part should -- all the condition -- all of the condition is that we have to hear that in private session. Yes, let's go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, I'm stating again that we are sitting pursuant to 15 bis, in the absence of Judge Lattanzi, who had to be away for urgent matters. Let's bring in the witness. While I'm cautious, because we are in public session, so, Mr. Karadzic, what is clear is that you can discuss it in public with any other witness, but not with this witness in public session. That's all. That's everything about the condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall I return this statement to the Prosecution? Good morning, General. I'm sorry for your inconvenience. There were some administrative matters to deal with in your absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're -- while the witness is getting settled, perhaps I could raise two matters quickly that the Court raised yesterday. First, you asked about the -- when we admitted 65 ter 04754, the agenda book for 1995, there was a -- the Court suggested that the agenda books be admitted in their entirety and asked whether they were encompassed by that 65 ter number. In fact, it appears that there is an agenda book for 1994 and one for 1996. 1994 is 65 ter 21460. 1996 is 65 ter 21459. So in accordance with the Court's inquiry, I wanted to alert you to that. And, secondly, you raised a question about the date of a document, but I'll clarify that if you're satisfied with the information provided with respect to the other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that question was with respect to 65 ter, I think it was, 03145. In any event, it became, I think, P2249. That was a Main Staff document. The transcript indicated that the date was identified as the 28th. You quite alertly looked to the date on the underlying document. And, in fact, both the underlying document and the B/C/S, and the English translation in e-court, both indicate a date of the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have to admit the other agendas at this moment. We'll admit them when tendered. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General Smith.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honour, should we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do that: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Once we're in private session, if I could just address you very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just want to make a motion for the record to exclude the testimony of General Smith, which is, I think, something formally we have to do so that later on, if this issue isn't resolved in any other way, we've preserved our objection. I would also ask the Prosecutor be directed to contact the United Nations again about this condition and ask them if they're really insisting, in light of the record and what was already public about this incident. They're usually very reasonable and place very few conditions. In fact, this is the only one that I'm aware of about public testimony at this trial. And I think if they understand the context, they might withdraw that condition, and that would be the best solution. So if that could be done. But failing all that, and if the testimony ends up being in private session throughout the duration of these proceedings, we feel that that's an infringement on Dr. Karadzic's right to a public trial and should result in the exclusion of the testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Robinson, I have to say that motion is too much belated. Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could call up 65 ter 01345.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tieger, I have to interrupt. To be clear, you don't suggest that we suspend the proceedings right now and consider your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would prefer that, actually. Yes, that would be the preferable thing to do, at least suspend the testimony with respect to this issue until it can be clarified whether the provider really insists. But that would be a very good suggestion, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know if it would be necessary to respond, and I'm pleased that there was a delay between hearing the motion to exclude and my response so I can be more temperate in my response, to what I will still say is a bizarrely overbroad motion, given the nature of the issue. If the question is whether the provider can be contacted before the Prosecution concludes its examination-in-chief, that's a physical impossibility, given the time difference. I will also indicate that while we're always prepared to assist the Court, we did seek reconsideration of this restriction previously. Now, whether or not the current circumstances and the extent to which the incident has been or is anticipated to be raised in public record - otherwise, it would have an impact on the provider - is another story, but that would seem to impact on the very practical ruling that the Court made, that should such restriction be lifted, then the testimony can become -- can then become public record. There's no -- it's difficult to see what advantage is -- under these circumstances is gained by not moving forward in the very practical way the Court just identified, parsing out thereafter what can be released publicly, even with the maintenance of the condition, and determining whether or not a full lifting of any condition can be obtained, thereby resulting in the complete release for public dissemination of the information. And the point of an adjournment would seem to be only delay. And I would again underscore that a motion to exclude this witness's testimony in its entirety based on this modest, limited condition is so far from well grounded as to be questionable in its intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise for 15 minutes to consider this matter. We will resume at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 9.43 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session. Oh, we are in private session. This is what my colleague Judge Baird said to me, that there's never a dull moment. The Chamber has listened to the argument raised by the Defence, as well as the position taken by the Prosecution, and it's surprised by the particular restriction being placed upon General Smith's testimony by the United Nations, particularly in light of the fact that the information about the four Serbs being taken prisoner appears to be already in the public domain. It may be in evidence in public in other cases and, indeed, in this case. Therefore, the Chamber encourages the Prosecution to immediately communicate with the United Nations concerning this restriction and to ask that it be lifted, given these circumstances. However, as the parties are aware, the Chamber can only accept the Rule 70 conditions placed on witness's testimony or exclude that testimony where it considers that the conditions imposed would undermine the need to ensure a fair trial and, subsequently, outweigh the testimony's probative value. The Chamber does not consideration that exclusion is warranted here, and, therefore, we will deny the motion and proceed to hear General Smith's evidence, going into private session when necessary to discuss the taking of these four Serb prisoners. However, as I indicated, once the testimony is completed, the Chamber will review the transcript and, in consultation with the Prosecution, may make certain portions public where it considers appropriate. Once again, it is our sincere hope that the United Nations will consent to the lifting of this particular restriction upon General Smith's testimony, and we ask that the Prosecution convey to the United Nations our concerns in this regard. Should the Rule 70 condition be lifted, the transcript can then be made public in its entirety. Mr. Tieger, we'll be expecting a progress report on your communication with the United Nations in due course. So we go back into open session and bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies again. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: General Smith, we're all sorry for the delay. I'm reminded, and perhaps you will understand that it is not just the British Army that fights all its battles uphill, at night, in the rain, at the junction of two maps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Welcome back, General. And, once again, I ask that we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And may we call up 65 ter 01345.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, while we're waiting for that document to come on screen, I'll just mention that, as a backdrop, we were discussing the hostage-taking and had earlier discussed a series of -- a number of phone calls you received during that period, and we are now turning to a record of phone calls from the -- a phone call from the 28th of May, 1995. We'll be briefly in private session because of a current restriction that may or may not be lifted, but it should have no impact on your testimony. And during the course of your cross-examination, there may be a further requirement to move into private session to discuss the detention of four Bosnian Serb prisoners, but that will be addressed as it arises. Meanwhile, I wanted to discuss with you, briefly, this telephone conversation between you and General Mladic on the 28th of May, 1995. And if we could turn the page, please. Just quickly running down some of the points there, and I want to give you a chance to review that: The document indicates that you initiated a 35-minute telephone conversation with General Mladic. Among the points discussed were the threats by the Bosnian Serbs to kill French soldiers unless the four Serbs detained following the incident on Vrbanja Bridge were released. You made a point, according to the document, that you would discuss exchange of all men detained once satisfied that Mladic had ceased threats to murder UN soldiers and that you had proof that UN personnel were not being used as human shields. We see, in the third paragraph, what appears to be an acknowledgment by General Mladic that it was true that some UN personnel were held at locations that were potential targets. And later in the discussion, there's a reference to Gorazde during a portion of the conversation, when General Mladic appears to be pressing for letters of condolence, and stating if you send them, you would be giving a chance for survival to the UK soldiers in Gorazde. And, finally, toward the end of the discussion, also noted an explanation by you to General Mladic that you were not in command of NATO, nor directing them, but was one of those responsible for recommending that an attack take place. General, I don't mean to usurp your recollection of that discussion or your identification of the salient points within that document, but wanted to touch on them briefly, as you were looking at it. Let me ask you first if, to the best of your recollection, this is generally a summary of that -- an accurate summary of that meeting and its salient points.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I just want to be clear about one thing you said. You said "UN shields." Did you mean the UN was being used as a shield, those soldiers that had been detained were being used as a shield?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I said UN soldiers were not being used as human shields.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, my --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But it was certainly a reference to the document, and --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was somewhere early on in what you said, and I wasn't sure what you meant by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think that would have been a reference to the middle of paragraph 2, which indicates: "General Smith restated his offer to discuss the exchange of all men detained once he was satisfied that Mladic had ceased his threats to murder UN soldiers and once he had proof that UNMOs and others were no longer used as human shields."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I was just looking for the bit in the document. Yes, it is a -- it is as I recollect that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And since it's been the subject of some discussion: What was the incident on Vrbanja Bridge?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early hours of that morning, I think it was, the -- an element of the Bosnian Serbs, dressed in French uniforms, that, I mean, I understood had been taken from men who had been captured earlier, approached the French position on the Vrbanja Bridge and attacked it -- took it by surprise, attacked it, captured some more men, and then there was a counter-attack shortly afterwards - I don't remember how long that took to mount - in which, I think, two French soldiers were killed, two Bosnian Serbs were killed, if recall correctly, and a number of wounded and two unwounded Bosnians were -- Bosnian Serbs were captured. I think there were two Bosnian Serb soldiers wounded, which gives you the four you've mentioned. There was then -- and this is in the aftermath. There's then -- a bit later on in the day, we get the threats to kill captured French soldiers unless the Bosnian Serb soldiers returned, and we start this -- then this telephone conversation comes from that, after that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender this document under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't object to it being admitted. We note that it's been admitted already as a public document, P342, in the Dragomir Milosevic case, and it's our position it shouldn't be under seal. But we understand your ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One clarification. Since we discussed it in private session, one may think that there should be no problem admitting this as a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I understand that -- and, again, I'm aware of the apparent discrepancy and inconsistency, but there is a condition on this particular document as well. It's not simply related -- it's independent of the testimony. And we will raise that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My point is this: There's no public record which shows that General Smith talked about this in public hearing, but when other witnesses are coming, for example, A or B, can discuss this document in public session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at the moment. And I attempted to make the distinction clear earlier that there was -- the two matters were, in fact, dealt with separately by the provider, the document and the testimony. And, by the way, I understood the Court's encouragement to the Prosecution to embrace both, and we'll be raising both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll think about this later on. Just I'll give you a very extreme example. Let's suppose just General Mladic is coming as a witness, which means that he cannot discuss it, this document, in public session. So we'll consider the matter later on. We'll proceed. We'll admit this under seal, and then we'll consider whether that status should continue later.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Exhibit P2269, temporarily under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could next call up 65 ter -- I'm sorry, we should move into open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could next call up 65 ter 21984.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, this is a document dated 29 May 1995, which is signed by you and appears to be titled "Post Air-Strike Guidance," and indicates in the first paragraph that you were writing the paper for two purposes: to provide an idea of the debate that is going on about you or around you, and, second, for direction. General, do you have this document, and can you indicate to the Court what it is about?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall the document. It -- you know, in the aftermath of the air-strikes, there was -- and the hostage-taking, there was a considerable debate developed, as it were, in Zagreb, New York, and the capitals of all those troop-contributing nations affected by this -- these events, and, of course, the North Atlantic Council of NATO. Much of this was not in my hearing, as it were, or I wasn't rung up about it or anything like that, but I was aware that it was going on and I was receiving quite a lot of information about it. And this -- and I was trying to see the way forward at the same time. So this document probably started as a mind-clearing exercise of my own, which I then thought might be more useful if I then distributed it. And I think I used the word "about" to mean it in both its senses, both about us, UNPROFOR, and around us, as UNPROFOR, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I used the -- as I say, the -- it then became a way of directing people's activities in the immediate future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you, in the course of that paper, identify short-term, medium-term, and long-term possibilities or objectives?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do. Certainly for the short/medium term, I think I do in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to, first, page 2 and then page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could we make it one click bigger, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, feel free to control the scrolling of the document, as well, as you need it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see in that paragraph 5 that I'm -- an example of what I understand is the argument going on behind us and above us. And then you see, in paragraph 7, that I have received some direction that is explicit and says that I am -- that my -- that the execution of the mandate I've been given is secondary to the security of UN personnel. And if we go on down. And there you see a list of our -- in the short term, what I propose to do. And then there's a third page, I'm sure. And I then list certain instructions. And I've already made a decision, on my own account, that we must start to reduce our exposure to the potential of the -- of having isolated detachments in that -- in the Bosnian Serb territory, and I am giving people the authority to abandon positions should the opportunity occur. I can't remember how many, but we had a number of little detachments at that stage still stuck in weapon collection points and surrounded. And I also have started to form a reaction force - I don't call it that then, but that's what it becomes - to -- and you see me here telling the sectors what to do and telling Sector South-West to prepare a battle group from their forces that they have under their command, with a particular task to prepare for, which is one of those weapon collection point detachments that's surrounded at that time. And then finally making the point that everyone's got to keep the pressure on the Bosnian government not to take advantage of these circumstances and, therefore, escalate the situation further. In the more medium term, I'm keen to establish some freedom of movement, and I tell the sector headquarters to prepare plans to use the forces that I've started to get them to assemble should they -- these opportunities occur -- to be used and should the opportunity occur. And then if we turn over. And I'm back with the eastern enclaves, and then I make the point that at this point of considerable stress on the force, with the troop-contributing nations getting very exercised about their own individual package of forces in the command, and the commanders of those -- the national commanders of those packages paying as much attention to their capital as they were to me, I finish by making clear that we've got to hang together here and be -- and although we're on the back foot at the moment, we must be prepared to be rather more offensive in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Your Honour, before I proceed, I know the schedule is disrupted today. I don't know exactly how the Court wishes to proceed, if it wishes to get back on the normal schedule or do something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about taking a 20 minutes' break for the first time. So we'll break in five minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thanks. General, you -- first of all, Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, you indicated that paragraph 7 reflects directions you received, that the execution of the mandate was secondary to the security of the UN personnel. Was that a response to the hostage-taking, and did that mean, in your view, that the hostage-taking had worked?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes to both questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you indicated yesterday that you had been advised at the outset and throughout that detained or captured UN personnel would be killed if air-strikes continued. Was it your understanding that that was the understanding throughout the UN about the plight of the hostages and what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely. I know we sent -- transmitted those threats back up our chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that that's what was -- that's what the Bosnian Serb authorities were trying to convey to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I have no doubt that the threats were being made, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look quickly at two exhibits. The first is 65 -- these are two intercepts, Your Honour. The first is 65 ter 30892. This is a conversation between Momcilo Vinkovic and Mr. Krajisnik on the 3rd of June, 1995. And looking at the first page, we see Vinkovic saying: "As long as you have hostages, you also have a trump card in your hands. Once you don't have them, you're finished." Later on on that page, he says: "I think that this played a great role, because they have stated and are openly writing and saying that they cannot do anything to you as long as you're holding hostages. They can't make a normal plan that they'll follow because every plan that they want to follow implies the use of military force, and they cannot do that because they'll endanger the lives of these hostages. Therefore, the hostages are of vital importance to you, regardless of what anyone else may be telling you." Krajisnik: "My dear man, we let some go and we captured some others." Vinkovic: "Keep doing that. That's all right, only you have to have some hostages at all times." Krajisnik: "All right, namesake. Everything is excellent, no doubt." And on the next page, if we scroll down a bit, Vinkovic again: "But, look, hold on to the hostages. That's a fantastic card. Don't ever forget that Saddam got destroyed when he released the hostages." Krajisnik: "Yes, yes. We're doing that. We have an excellent method. We always have an ace up our sleeve." And, very quickly, one more before we break. That's 65 ter 30890, and I'll be tendering them both to be marked for identification, Your Honour, in just a moment. First, let's look at 30890.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have a say about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About the admission, I hope you will give me an opportunity, before your decision, to state my opinion about this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we turn to page 2, we see, at the top, a reference to Kozyrev and the -- as the interlocutor Momcilo says to him,

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Yes, he says that you are barbarians because you tied the blue helmets to the bridges ...," et cetera. And then as the conversation continues, in the middle of the page, Momcilo urges negotiating everything, just not the hostages: "The holding of hostages is a new way of waging war. You hold hostages as protection. Don't believe any promises. They have lied before, they will lie again. Therefore, the hostages are a guarantee ..." And, finally, quickly turning to the next page, toward the bottom: "I saw a tied-up UNPROFOR coward." This is Momcilo speaking: "They asked him how they were being treated. He said, 'Very well,' that they were taken to sleep at night and then brought back during the day. In fact, he told NATO that the targets were unprotected at night and that they could strike." Momcilo: "Yes, yes, but tomorrow we'll ..." Momcilo: "Look, put them into eight-hour shifts. They are rotten, they have very good devices for night-time bombardment." Krajisnik: "Good. I think that they saw clearly what would happen to them so that they have to take care."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, are those conversations involving Mr. Krajisnik consistent with your understanding of the threats to the safety of the hostages that were presented to you if the air-strikes did not cease?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are of a piece, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those documents, Your Honour, for identification at this point, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to say that in addition to our very well-known position about intercepts, I think it would be very useful for Mr. Tieger to inform us who the collocutors are, whether this is an official conversation, et cetera. It is of crucial importance, who Krajisnik is trying to impress and who the collocutors are. And, if necessary, I can assist him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, if -- I'm happy to receive information from Mr. Karadzic, through Mr. Robinson, on that score. However, this is not the time for arguing the weight to be given these intercepts. They should be admitted in the customary fashion, and the accused will be free, at a more appropriate time, to argue his view of what weight it should be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, Mr. Tieger. But it's important to find out who the interlocutors are, and we'll be assisted to know who they are, but it's not at this time. We'll mark it for identification, both of them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2271 and MFI P2272, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise for a break, and we'll resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me turn next to 65 ter 19294.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, I wanted to direct your attention to a record of a meeting involving General Janvier with General Mladic on the 4th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I guess the document needs to be released, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, you now see before you the document, which indicates at the outset that there were four main discussion points: UN personnel being held as hostages; replenishment of the eastern enclaves; UN ascendance; and Serbian air-space. And let me just quickly direct your attention to a couple of those before I ask any questions. The first page reflects General Janvier addressing the UN personnel as hostages issue, and characterising it at the outset as unacceptable; in the second paragraph indicating to General Mladic that he is practically -- that the Bosnian Serbs are practically banishing themselves from the international community, referring to one of the consequence, both direct and irreversible, being the imminent arrival of the multinational brigade to increase security for the blue helmets; the third paragraph further discussing the discrediting impact of the action and comparing it to Saddam Hussein. If we move on to the second page. There is -- General Janvier continues talking about the hostages, but then moves into the subject of replenishment of the eastern enclaves, and begins by noting that the eastern enclaves are in urgent need of replenishment: "The situation has become intolerable. Soldiers located there are in need of food and fuel." And he continues, in the later paragraph, stressing the urgency of the circumstances and the need for imminent advancement, noting, at the bottom of that page: "This is a matter of such urgency that a significant advancement must be made within the next two or three days." The third point, which is titled "UN Ascendancy," addresses weapons collection points as a particular problem falling under that category, noting that the withdrawal of armament by the Bosnian Serbs from the positions they occupy is irreversible, but the armament must be taken out of the exclusion zone. And then the fourth point deals with air-space. We'll note, as we turn the page, that General Mladic's positions are then reflected later in the document. General Mladic stresses at the outset, according to this document, the need for a guarantee regarding air-strikes and their cessation, not only then, but permanently and in the future. As we continue down the page, in the penultimate paragraph on that page, it also reflects General Mladic's insistence on the lifting of sanctions of all Serbian people in the world, liberation of all detained, the de-blocking of assets, and so on. First of all, General Smith, let me ask you if you were aware of this specific meeting or the discussions that took place at the meeting at the time.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the meeting that was going to take place and that it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do the positions outlined in this document accord with your understanding of the positions of the UN and the positions of General Mladic or the Bosnian Serbs at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, rather, yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to -- in light of the discussion about urgent need for replenishment and the continuing issue of convoys and convoy restrictions, can I turn quickly to two documents in late June. The first would be 65 ter 11339. Sorry, General, just one moment. Perhaps we could try 11338. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document, an inter-office memo, dated the 26th of June, 1995, reflecting a meeting that you had with Colonel Meille on that date, and begins by noting that Colonel Meille explained that for the third time that morning, a French convoy on Igman was engaged by a Serb cannon and a tank: "The Serbs seemed determined to prevent us from using this road by constantly harassing our convoys." And then there's a discussion about possible response, and limitations on that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn the page so the General could see the full document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I don't know if you recall this specific incident, but can you tell us whether or not this is a continuation of the problem that you have been describing regarding efforts to provide resupply and/or humanitarian assistance for the civilian population to either of the enclaves of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In June, after the air-strikes, the only route into Sarajevo available to bring supplies in was over the Igman trail, and this was how we were moving ourselves and escorting in UNHCR convoys. I can't remember when it started, but over June, the incidence of these convoys being engaged by fire from Bosnian Serb positions increased. And this is a -- I've gone down and I'm clearly in the French -- in the sector headquarters -- Sector South-West headquarters, and we were discussing where we'd go next. We've tried various methods, and this is a discussion of what now to do. The reference in the document on the screen to the UNTF, A and B, are those two battle groups that I ordered being formed in that document that I was shown before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P2274.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This is in evidence. It's Exhibit P2116.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, we're about to move into late June and early July. I wanted to ask you one additional question about the restriction on humanitarian aid or resupply convoys. Yesterday, we addressed -- or you addressed a number of meetings you had with Dr. Karadzic or with General Mladic where the issue of convoy restrictions and freedom of movement was discussed. I think it was at 11321. You also looked at a section of the Supreme Command directive issued in March 1995 by Dr. Karadzic, which outlined a policy of restricting resupply convoys to UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid to the Muslim population. And there, you said: "It's clearly a central direction. Here is a high-level order being issued to carry this -- these actions out." I wanted to ask you who you understood was ultimately responsible -- that is, what political or military figure was ultimately responsible for this policy of convoy restrictions.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I understood it as being General Mladic. And the person who is dealing with General Mladic at that time, because I wasn't because of the hostages being taken, was General Janvier. And if I recall correctly, either as a result of the meeting you've -- we've discussed already or another one, a convoy was organised from Serbia into the enclaves, but I may have got that -- it may have been at a later date, but I think it happened in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the numerous meetings you held with Dr. Karadzic, what was the purpose of those meetings and what did you consider his role in the issue of convoy restrictions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall meeting him in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I was referring to the entire --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Referring to the discussions yesterday, the meetings we were talking about yesterday, the entire subject of convoy restrictions, beginning from the time that you undertook your command to the end.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm clearly -- I mean, we discussed the business of supplying the enclaves, that's Dr. Karadzic and I. And if -- I had an understanding in the -- that the policy was emanating from the whole -- the top of the Bosnian Serb leadership, which would have included the president and Mladic, but the operative restrictions and, therefore, the -- and the person who had to sort of give -- whose forces were the controlling element that one needed to deal with was General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. There's an "if" in that answer that I'm not sure that was intended, so let me see if I have a correct understanding of what you just said. And that is: The policy emanated from the top of the Bosnian Serb leadership, meaning Dr. Karadzic, and along with General Mladic as the operative controller of that policy, the person who was implementing that policy that emanated from the top; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, that the -- the point of call, as it were, for dealing with convoys was through Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I'd like to turn next to 65 ter 01356.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we can see on screen, General Smith, this is a letter dated the 26th of June, 1995, to General Mladic, and signed by you. And at the beginning, indicating that you're writing further to a letter sent by your chief of staff concerning Srebrenica, and wishing to express your increasing concern about a sequence of very serious incidents. And you refer, in paragraph 2, to the fact that on an almost daily basis, you were receiving reports of shelling of the populated areas of Bihac, Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Sarajevo, and refer to what happened the previous day in Sarajevo, with nine civilians, among them five children, being killed due to sniping and shelling. You also provide a reminder about the safe area regime, pursuant to the Security Council resolution. And in addition to your concern about the attacks on the civilian population, you also note an increasing number of reports of direct targeting of UNPROFOR locations and vehicles in various locations. Do you recall sending this, General, do you recall the circumstances at the time, and do you recall what response, if any, you received from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall -- I remember sending this letter, and I -- but I don't recall the response that it received. And I'm -- and I think I must have been trying to put in one document the situation as it was towards the end of that month and the -- and wanted to be clear, just because we'd been in circumstances where the resolution about safe areas couldn't be discharged, that didn't mean to say that continuing to attack the people in the safe areas was permissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I appreciate that after this period of time, you may not be expected to recall the specific response you received from General Mladic. Let me ask you this: Can you tell us whether you received any indication from General Mladic, in response to your expression of concerns about these serious matters, that there would be a reversal of what had been happening and that the attacks on the civilian population and upon UNPROFOR locations and troops would stop?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that being -- occurring at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, we're moving into July, in terms of our time-frame, and, therefore, close to the time of Srebrenica. I understand that you were on leave at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although in contact via radio link, you weren't in theatre, at the least at the beginning of the month?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall how you began to be apprised of events developing in Srebrenica at the beginning of July and as it moved into the commencement of the attack on the enclave and the taking of Srebrenica by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is that the -- I was recalled off leave to go to Geneva in the -- of the two weeks I was on -- planned to be on leave at the weekend -- the middle weekend of this -- of that period. And we flew up to Geneva, where the Secretary-General was discussing the report on the UNPROFOR in the Balkans. During that meeting, I think right at the end, we were told that an attack was developing on Srebrenica and a Dutch soldier had been killed. The understanding of what was going on that was transmitted to us was that this was a local attack in response to a raid that had been conducted by the Bosnians a day or two before, in which a number of Bosnian Serbs had been killed and, I seem to recall, sheep and so forth had been stolen. I was told that I didn't need to return and I was to go back off on leave, so I did. At some point, I think, on the Monday, which from my memory was the 10th, the -- things had begun to reach a point, in that I was being rung up very frequently, or, rather, radioed very frequently as to what was going on. And on the 11th, I was -- came back off leave and started the fairly prolonged process of getting back into Sarajevo. I think I arrived on the morning -- very early hours of the morning of the 13th. I had, either on -- I think it was in the morning of the 11th or evening of the 11th, I had a number of telephone calls with people, because I was going through Split at that time. I may have got my date wrong by one day either way, but I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would -- I don't know if this refreshes your recollection and -- well, we can check. There's a reference in your amalgamated statement to: "I arrived back at BH Command in the early hours of the evening 12 July." But it seems like the time-frame is roughly --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, let me show you a document that was issued from UNPROFOR Command HQ on the 9th of July, and that would be 65 ter 03923. It indicates that they have sent it as a CapSat to General Mladic and will issue it as a press statement. And if we could turn the page, please. It's entitled: "Warning to the Bosnian Serbs, attacks against the Srebrenica safe area." And commences: "The Bosnian Serb Army resumed attacks against the Srebrenica enclave on Friday, 7 July 1995, firing indiscriminately into the safe area and directly targeting UN facilities, causing several civilian deaths." And it goes on to describe what happened following the concerted attack against the UN OP at Zeleni Jadar on the 8th and so on. The second paragraph indicates that: "This attack against a UN-declared safe area is totally unacceptable and represents a grave escalation of the conflict." And demands that the advance stop and that the Bosnian Serb Army withdraw to the perimeter of the demilitarised zone. And the document has a time code, it appears at the top, of 2220 hours. That would be 10.20 in the evening, I take it. And there's a fax indication of 2232 above. General, were you aware of the issuance of this warning to the Bosnian Serbs on that date?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I was told about it in one of those radio calls, but I -- I don't remember its substances in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is part of the process of receiving information and responding to it during the time-frame that you describe?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, one moment. I want to direct your attention to something that happened at approximately the same time on the 9th of July. That's 65 ter 01903.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's also dated the 9th. As you can see, it emanates from the Main Staff of the army, signed by -- or General Tolimir's name appears at the bottom. And from the stamp at the top, it indicates that it was not only the 9th of July, but sent at 2350 hours, so around the time or approximately an hour and a half after that document we looked at a moment ago. And it refers -- is sent to the Drina Corps Command, refers to the fact that the president of Republika Srpska had been informed of the successful combat operations that achieved results, enabling the units of the Drina Corps to occupy the very town of Srebrenica; that the president is satisfied with the results of the combat operations and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave. And then it goes on to describe the president's order regarding the follow-up com -- operations, including protection for UNPROFOR members and the civilian Muslim population, and refraining from destroying civilian targets unless forced to do so, et cetera, et cetera. First of all, General, do you recall whether UNPROFOR Command was aware of not necessarily the specific document, but the continuation of operations beyond the occupation of the very town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I don't think people understood that this attack, in my headquarters, would lead to the complete collapse of the pocket or enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We're happy to have this admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, General, just before I leave this document: Note, at the bottom of the document, Tolimir directing that: "In accordance with the order of the president of Republika Srpska, you must issue an order ... to offer maximum protection and safety ... order subordinate units to refrain from destroying civilian targets ... ban the torching of residential buildings, and treat the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions ..." I wanted to ask you, if a commander is -- in order to ensure compliance with the Geneva Conventions or if the commander is concerned about non-compliance with the Geneva Conventions, is the issuing of an order sufficient to address that ?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I object to that, both as for calling -- for invading the province of the Chamber on a legal issue and calling for expert testimony for which this witness has not been authorised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. Do you have a response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, it certainly doesn't invade the province of the Court, and this institution has welcomed and invited the assistance of witnesses who bring to the Chamber a mixture of fact and experience and can shed light on operative events, documents, and so on. And I think that this falls well within the ambit of that jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not as an expert. Based upon his experience, the Chamber is of the view that the witness can express his view, if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't find it remarkable that an instruction such as that, to pay attention to the Geneva Conventions in this case, appears in an order. I can think of lots of occasions when that has or something similar has occurred. But an order is only an order. It has to be executed and supervised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could turn next, please, to 65 ter 2119 -- 21119, if I missed a 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, as you see, this is a document dated the 13th of July, 1995, and reflects a meeting that you had with Prime Minister Silajdzic on the 13th of July, during which the situation in Srebrenica, the refugee crisis, and unconfirmed reports of atrocities, were discussed. And if I could turn your attention quickly to point 6 of this document. That indicates that both the prime minister and Minister Muratovic raised concerns about the as-yet unconfirmed reports of atrocities in the Srebrenica area, in particular rape of young women and murder of a bus-load of refugees. And they also expressed, as we see later in that paragraph, concern about reports of refugees being segregated into groups, and men between the ages of 16 and 60 being sent to different locations. General, do you recall hearing concerns at this time about atrocities and information about the separation of military-age men from others?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These -- we were beginning to hear such accounts, yes, and not -- we had reports other than the ones in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn next to -- oh, I ask this document be admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to 65 ter 01689. This is the -- contains the commander of UNPROFOR -- that is, your assessment and recommendations arising from the fall of Srebrenica. And if we could turn the page, please. It indicates at the outset that in the aftermath of the fall of Srebrenica, issue arise; and the two immediate matters, in particular, the reception and care of refugees and the recovery of DutchBat. You note in paragraph 2 that: "The Bosnian Serbs are intent on moving fast to present a fait accompli. They wish to remove the enclaves, inter alia, to free their rear area, to provide troops for a decisive blow and possibly to counter the Rapid Reaction Force." In paragraph 3, you indicate that the Bosnian Serbs are, quote: "... 'cleansing' Srebrenica. DutchBat are doing what they can to monitor to the situation, but reports of abductions and murder, unconfirmed as yet, are beginning to be heard. Men of military age are being separated from the refugees." You go on, in the next page, about the need to recover DutchBat, and then talk about, below that, available options. And if we could scroll down so the General can see the entire document. And turn the page, which contains the small remainder of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, as always, you're free to look at any portion of the document or peruse it for whatever time needed. But let me ask you if you recall preparing this document and what it reflected.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could I see the front page? I just -- my memory is that I dictated it fairly late on the 13th. So it went out, yes, just before midnight. I am -- this is the end of my first day back in Srebrenica, and I'm trying to get a grip of the situation and inform the -- and to try and inform the process of deciding what we, the UN, are going to do about this by telling Mr. Akashi, and the force commander and so forth, how I see the situation and what the immediate concerns are. At that time, those are what I think are the immediate concerns, and I am particularly trying to get across at one stage that the Bosnian government is endeavouring to load, if you like, the whole problem of dealing with the refugees on us, and that we are going to have to set up a base to handle all these people - again, we didn't know the numbers at this stage - and so on. And then there's the -- as to how we deal with the DutchBat, who are stuck with a number of people detained by the Bosnian Serbs, as well as the whole battalion still stuck in Sarajevo, how do I get them out. And the commanding officer of the battalion is the -- is not really in a position to negotiate this, since he's, as it were -- I think I used the phrase somewhere in there "he is talking from the jail," he is inside the problem, not on the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I then describe what I think are the alternatives before us, and that if we don't act, ourselves, it will be -- events will just fall into what I seem to recall I called lying back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe that reference to talking from the jail can be found in the third sentence of paragraph 4. General, you noted earlier that by the 13th you were beginning to hear accounts of atrocities and the separation of military-age men from others, and you said: "We had reports, other than the ones in the document we were looking at." Do you recall some of those other reports?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I'm making reference to the reports from DutchBat, which were limited, but that's the only other place, other than the Bosnian government, that I recall receiving those reports from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the -- by the end of -- by July 13th or by the end of that date, did you understand, from the information you'd been receiving, whether or not there had been a break-out by defenders, irrespective of the particular numbers involved?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, and I'm not -- I don't know whether I make reference to that in this document. What we know is we can't account for the defenders. I think we have an understanding that there's -- there is a group of some 2.000 people who we know have been moved to a football pitch, but I -- that may have come in the following 24 hours. I'm not sure of my times in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you recall the location where the 2.000 people you referred to were moved to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bratunac, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could tender the document we were just reviewing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, I'd like to move to the 15th and to an entry in the Mladic note-books that reflects a meeting with General Mladic, President Milosevic, and others that we will see. That's P1488, page 4 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: General, here we see a meeting -- the title is: "Meeting with UN and Milosevic." It's dated Saturday, 15July 1995, and indicates that those present were Stoltenberg, Akashi, Bildt, General De Lapresle and yourself. Do you recall that -- and that there was a separate meeting with De Lapresle and General Smith?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can scroll down, I wanted to ask you some questions about what's contained there. I'm sorry, the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference there to: "Allow access to all prisoners for ICRC." Was there a push by yourself and other UN officials for the ICRC to get access to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were -- we were -- we wanted access for the ICRC and UNHCR to all the detained people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was conveyed to General Mladic at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Looking down further in the page, there's a reference, under your name, to the treatment of the population in Srebrenica and Zepa and to the rumours about atrocities, massacres and rapes. If we look further on the page -- the next page, rather, it continues: "It would be good if you would allow the UNHCR and IRC/International Red Cross as soon as possible." General, did you and/or others at the meeting convey your concerns about information you were getting concerning massacres and atrocities against the Bosnian Muslims, and continue to press for ICRC access to determine whether that was accurate, and to protect the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And I'm confident I didn't use the word "rumour." I'm much more likely to have said "it is alleged" or, "I have received reports that ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's turn next to 65 ter 01690.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an outgoing code cable dated the 17th of July, 1995, and it has attached the summary of some of the main points discussed at the meeting, indicating also that you and Mladic had a long bilateral discussion. If we could turn to the next page, please. And looking at the fourth point under the Srebrenica section, it indicates: "ICRC to have immediate access to 'prisoners of war,'" that's in quotes, "to assess their welfare, register, and review procedures at Bosnian Serb reception centre in accordance with the Geneva Convention." Is this a further reflection, General, of the importance that you and other international officials attached to the need to get the ICRC in to see what was happening and to protect those who were prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
